issues.legal_issue: A law imposing ceilings on agricultural holdings and distributing surplus land is agrarian reform legislation protected from fundamental-rights challenges.
material_facts: The legislation imposed ceilings on agricultural holdings and provided for acquiring and distributing surplus land to landless and weaker sections of society.
The legislation was enacted to give effect to the principles concerning distribution of material resources and prevention of concentration of wealth.
issues.conclusion: The legislation, including its amendments, was in substance agrarian reform and fell within the constitutional protection for such legislation, making it immune from challenges based on fundamental rights concerning equality, property, and related freedoms.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 31A, legislation that in substance concerns agrarian reform is protected against challenges based on Articles 14, 19, and 31. The Court relied on Sankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India, Keshavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, and State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh.

predicates.agrarian_land_ceiling_case: The proceeding challenges legislation that imposes ceilings on agricultural landholdings.
predicates.surplus_land_is_acquired_for_redistribut: The legislation provides for acquiring surplus agricultural land and distributing it to landless or weaker sections.

issues.definition: When a proceeding challenges an agricultural land-ceiling scheme that acquires surplus land for redistribution, the scheme receives protection as agrarian reform legislation.

issues.legal_issue: Only measures included in the protected constitutional schedule receive that schedule's immunity, and subordinate rules not included there do not receive it merely because the parent legislation is included.
material_facts: The principal legislation and one amending enactment were included in the protected constitutional schedule.
Later amending enactments were not included in that schedule.
The land-ceiling rules were subordinate legislation and were not specified in the schedule.
issues.conclusion: The principal legislation and the amendment included in the schedule received its protection; the later amendments and the rules did not receive that protection on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31B protects enactments specified in the Ninth Schedule. The Court relied on Prag Ice and Oil Mills v. Union of India in explaining that subordinate legislation not specified in the schedule does not thereby obtain the same protection.

rule.if: schedule_protection_case and measure_is_in_protected_schedule and not measure_is_unscheduled_subordinate_rule

predicates.schedule_protection_case: The proceeding concerns whether a challenged legal measure receives protection by virtue of its inclusion in a constitutionally protected schedule.
predicates.measure_is_in_protected_schedule: The challenged measure is specified in the protected constitutional schedule.
predicates.measure_is_unscheduled_subordinate_rule: The challenged measure is subordinate legislation that is not itself specified in the protected schedule.

issues.definition: A challenged measure receives schedule immunity when it is specified in the protected schedule and is not an unscheduled subordinate rule.

issues.legal_issue: An artificial family definition and different ceiling treatment for a family unit and an adult son living with that unit do not violate equality where the distinctions are supported by the agrarian policy and the legislation's objectives.
material_facts: The legislation treated a family as a husband, wife, and their minor children, and treated an adult son living with his parents as a separate unit.

The permissible area could increase for additional family members and for an adult son living with the family, but not for an unmarried daughter living with the family or an adult son living separately.

The State submitted policy materials explaining the choice of family as the operative unit, the need to prevent evasion through transfers to relatives, and the different treatment of adult sons living with the family.
The policy materials addressed rural agricultural practice and the capacity of a family to cultivate land personally.
issues.conclusion: The artificial definition and double standard were not unconstitutional; the policy justification was sufficient to repel the equality challenge, and the legislation's agrarian-reform character also brought it within constitutional protection.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 14 and Article 31A. It distinguished Karimbil Kunhikoman v. State of Kerala and A.P. Krishnasami Naidu v. State of Madras because those enactments lacked the relevant protection and the States had not supplied comparable justification. It also held that an agrarian-reform enactment is not invalid merely because it omits provision for an exceptional or rare case.

predicates.family_unit_ceiling_case: The proceeding challenges a land-ceiling scheme that uses a family unit to determine permissible agricultural holdings.
predicates.policy_material_supports_the_family_unit: The State presents material explaining why the family is treated as the operative unit for applying the ceiling and preventing evasion.
predicates.policy_material_supports_differential_tr: The State presents material explaining why the scheme treats members living with the family differently from those living separately or in other circumstances.

issues.definition: A family-based ceiling classification is valid when the State's material supports both the use of the family unit and the distinctions drawn within that scheme.

issues.legal_issue: Giving the husband authority to make the family's land-retention selection does not discriminate against the wife when retained land remains owned in the same proportions as before selection.
material_facts: The husband was authorized to make the family declaration and select the land to be retained as permissible area.
The land retained for the family and separate unit had to be owned or held by their members in the same proportions as before the selection.
The challenge alleged that the husband could select his own land and cause the wife's land to be treated as surplus.
issues.conclusion: The selection arrangement did not discriminate against the wife because the retained land had to preserve the members' prior ownership proportions.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 14 together with the statutory requirement that ownership of the retained permissible area remain in the same proportions as before selection.

predicates.family_land_selection_case: The proceeding challenges a land-retention selection made for a family under a ceiling scheme.
predicates.one_spouse_selects_retained_land: One spouse is authorized to submit the family's declaration and select which land is retained.
predicates.retained_land_preserves_prior_ownership_: The members' ownership shares in the retained land remain proportionate to their ownership shares before selection.

issues.definition: A spouse's authority to select retained land is not discriminatory when the retained land preserves the family's prior ownership proportions.

issues.legal_issue: Ignoring a prohibited post-cutoff transfer when calculating surplus land does not discriminate against a spouse whose land may consequently be treated as surplus.
material_facts: The legislation prohibited specified transfers of land after the applicable cutoff and required a prohibited transfer to be ignored when calculating permissible and surplus areas.
The challenge alleged that clubbing family holdings could cause the wife's land to become surplus when the husband made a prohibited transfer.
The Court reasoned that the transferor risked having his own land disregarded and the affected land vest in the State.
issues.conclusion: The challenge to the treatment of prohibited transfers failed; the consequences did not establish discrimination against the wife.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 14 and upheld the rule that a prohibited transfer is ignored when calculating the permissible and surplus areas, noting that the transferor's conduct could jeopardize the land involved and cause it to vest in the State.

predicates.family_land_transfer_case: The proceeding challenges how a land-ceiling scheme treats transfers involving a family holding.
predicates.transfer_contravenes_the_ceiling_scheme: A person makes a transfer that the ceiling scheme prohibits.
predicates.transfer_is_ignored_in_surplus_calculati: The scheme requires the prohibited transfer to be disregarded when determining permissible and surplus holdings.

issues.definition: The treatment of a prohibited transfer is not discriminatory when the scheme disregards it in calculating surplus land.

issues.legal_issue: Rules that supply the method for evaluating mixed categories of agricultural land do not exceed the legislature's authority when the legislation itself fixes the land categories and permissible areas.
material_facts: The legislation divided land into categories and specified the permissible area for each category.
The legislation left the method of evaluating holdings to prescribed rules.
The rules supplied a conversion formula between land categories and a method using irrigation intensity to determine the extent of land in different categories.
The challenged rule was alleged to reduce the permissible area fixed by the legislation and to reverse the function of the other evaluation rule.
issues.conclusion: The challenged evaluation rule was valid; the legislation fixed the permissible areas, while the rules provided the evaluation method and operated on different aspects of that calculation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that fixing the permissible area was done by the legislation and that prescribing the basis for evaluating land was a permissible role for rules. It read the evaluation rules together, treating one as providing the conversion formula and the other as identifying category amounts using irrigation intensity.

predicates.land_ceiling_rule_challenge: The proceeding challenges a rule used to calculate permissible and surplus agricultural holdings.
predicates.parent_law_fixes_categories_and_permissi: The governing legislation itself identifies land categories and fixes the permissible area for each category.
predicates.rules_supply_only_the_evaluation_method: The challenged rules provide a method for evaluating land holdings rather than fixing the underlying permissible areas.

issues.definition: An evaluation rule is valid when the legislation fixes the categories and permissible areas and the rule supplies only the method for evaluating holdings.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation for surplus land is not illusory where the payable rates reflect the land's actual quality and yield and the challenger supplies no material showing otherwise.
material_facts: The legislation provided rates for calculating payment for surplus land vested in the State.
The rates were based on the actual quality of the soil and its yield.
No material was placed before the Court to show that the rates produced illusory compensation.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the challenge that the compensation was illusory.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the compensation provision by reference to the statutory rates and the evidence presented, finding that rates based on soil quality and yield were not shown to be illusory.

predicates.surplus_land_compensation_case: The proceeding challenges the payment provided for land taken as surplus under a land-ceiling scheme.
predicates.compensation_rates_reflect_land_quality_: The payment rates are based on the quality and yield of the land.
predicates.no_material_shows_compensation_is_illuso: The challenger provides no material demonstrating that the payment is illusory.

issues.definition: Compensation is not shown to be illusory when its rates reflect land quality and yield and no contrary supporting material is provided.

issues.legal_issue: A condition requiring security for an appeal or revision concerning surplus land is valid if it is not so onerous as to make the statutory remedy nearly illusory.
material_facts: The legislation conditioned an appeal or revision against a surplus-land determination on a deposit or bank guarantee linked to the disputed area.
The amount was related to land tax, and the legislation provided for adjustment or return of the security depending on the outcome.
The condition was intended to discourage frivolous appeals and revisions that would impede implementation of the ceiling scheme.
The Court considered the condition modest in light of the tax basis and the disputed area to which it applied.
issues.conclusion: The condition was not so onerous or unreasonable as to invalidate the appeal and revision remedies.
issues.legal_principle: A statutory right of appeal may be made subject to conditions so long as they are not unreasonably onerous and do not make the right almost illusory. The Court applied Anant Mills Ltd. v. State of Gujarat and considered the purpose, tax-based measure, scope, and treatment of the security.

predicates.surplus_land_appeal_or_revision_case: The proceeding challenges a condition attached to an appeal or revision against a surplus-land determination.
predicates.security_is_limited_to_the_disputed_area: The required security is calculated only by reference to the land area disputed in the appeal or revision.
predicates.security_is_proportionate_and_recoverabl: The security is modest in relation to the relevant tax and is returned, released, or adjusted according to the outcome.

issues.definition: A security condition is not unreasonable when it is confined to the disputed area, proportionate, and treated according to the outcome.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge that a rule concerning prohibited transfers violates the agrarian-reform protection is barred where the governing legislation and that rule are protected by inclusion in the constitutional schedule.
material_facts: The challenged transfer provision formed part of the land-ceiling legislation.
The legislation was included in the protected constitutional schedule.
The appellants argued that the provision violated a limitation associated with the constitutional protection for agrarian-reform laws.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the provision received the schedule's protection and did not decide the challenge on its merits under the agrarian-reform limitation.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31B protects legislation included in the Ninth Schedule. The Court treated that protection as sufficient to dispose of this challenge, without separately deciding the asserted limitation on the agrarian-reform protection.

predicates.scheduled_land_ceiling_law_challenge: The proceeding challenges a provision of a land-ceiling law that is included in a constitutionally protected schedule.
predicates.challenged_transfer_rule_is_part_of_sche: The challenged rule concerning transfers forms part of the scheduled land-ceiling law.

issues.definition: A challenge to a transfer provision is defeated by schedule protection when the provision forms part of a land-ceiling law included in the protected schedule.
